Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Elena Morales had been reviewing supplier contracts in a sub-basement storage unit when the heavy steel door clicked shut behind the foreman. She remembered the sound distinctly, a metallic finality that echoed through the narrow aisle of stacked crates. For three days, the maintenance crew forgot to check the interior camera feeds, leaving her in that locked room. She could not open the heavy lever lock from the inside, and the narrow clearance offered no clear path forward. The weight of having no options settled over her; every time she considered climbing onto the rolling ladder, she would lower herself back down, convinced that waiting was safer than risking a misstep. When the foreman finally returned, he found her stiff, her hands gripping the seam of her jacket, a sharp, persistent ache radiating down the left side of her neck. In the weeks that followed, Elena found herself carrying that sub-basement stillness into her project management office at the logistics firm. The glass-walled conference rooms, when the doors were pushed closed for client calls, suddenly felt like extensions of that storage unit. She began leaving the heavy doors ajar, though she knew they were no different from the unlocked doors at the warehouse. Her neck pain did not fade with time; instead, it settled into a familiar companion, flaring whenever she leaned over engineering blueprints to point out a structural discrepancy. She would press her fingertips to the tense muscles at the base of her skull, certain that the stiffness was proof the event had not been a temporary inconvenience. Her mind began turning over the capture in slow, deliberate loops. She replayed the foreman's distracted glance, the exact angle of the dropped key, the way the overhead light had failed to catch the latch. What frightened her most was the possibility that she had somehow failed to secure the exit properly, that her oversight had invited the confinement. She would catch herself whispering to her apartment plants that the whole ordeal was merely a minor delay, a trick of the building's acoustics, as if speaking the doubt away could erase it. Her life in the years after her divorce settled into a steady rhythm of co-occurring sensations. Even inside her own home, Elena remained on guard. She would pause with the kettle in hand, listening to the refrigerator cycle, suddenly convinced a floorboard outside her bedroom window had shifted. She was unable to relax, even when she knew the streets were quiet, her shoulders perpetually drawn up as though bracing for a door to latch. False alarms accumulated with the grocery receipts; a dropped pen on the subway made her jump, a neighbor's heavy footsteps on the stairwell sent a quick pulse to her neck. A score of 77 on her intake survey mirrored the quiet arithmetic of her days. She had come to believe that happiness was something she possessed before the capture, something that required uninterrupted air and open doors, but now she felt a steady emotional numbness settle behind her ribs, as though the world had been filtered through frosted glass. The fear of harm was no longer tied to the foreman or the building; it lived in the uncertainty of strangers, in the simple truth that you could never know who would harm you next. She watched her colleagues pack up for the weekend, her colleagues laughing near the copy room, and she felt the familiar weight of misalignment, neither explaining it to her manager nor expecting them to understand. At fifty-nine, Elena finally scheduled an intake after her latest quarterly review. During the meeting, a junior analyst had accidentally turned the heavy conference room door to the locked position while handing her a tablet. Elena had sat perfectly still, her neck aching, her thoughts circling the same questions of responsibility and overlooked details, waiting to see who would come to open it. The delay did not break her, but it crystallized what she had been carrying. She had come to seek help not because the pain in her shoulders had become unbearable, but because she was tired of the quiet constant of bracing. What she hoped for was simply the return of unforced ease, the ability to walk through a room and trust that the latch would hold only when it needed to.
